3.5.paragraph: Honeybees cannot talk, but they can share information about food. When a bee {fi|nds} good flowers, it {fl|ies} back to the hive and {do|es} a special {da|nce}. If the food is very {cl|ose}, the bee moves in small {cir|cles}. If the food is far away, it does a "waggle dance" and {sha|kes} its body in a straight line. The {dire|ction} of this line shows other bees {wh|ere} to fly. The {lon|ger} the bee shakes, the farther away the food is.

4.5.paragraph: Honeybees use dances to tell their nestmates where to find food. A forager that discovers {flo|wers} close to the hive performs a round dance, {circ|ling} first one way and then the other. For more {dis|tant} food, it performs a waggle dance on the {vert|ical} surface of the honeycomb. The angle of the waggle run {comp|ared} with straight up matches the {an|gle} between the food and the sun. The {len|gth} of each run signals {dist|ance}, and a more {ener|getic} dance often {indi|cates} a richer source.

5.5.paragraph: Honeybee foragers communicate the location of resources through a remarkably precise symbolic language of dances. On the vertical comb, a returning {for|ager} performs a waggle run whose {orien|tation} relative to gravity {corre|sponds} to the angle between the {nec|tar} source and the sun's {azi|muth}. Because the sun {shi|fts} across the sky, dancers {grad|ually} adjust this angle throughout the day. The {dura|tion} of each run encodes distance, while the vigor and {repet|ition} of the dance convey the {profit|ability} of the site, recruiting more workers to superior patches.

shared.title: Trade Along the Silk Road
shared.text:
The Silk Road was not a single road but a vast network of overland routes that connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean world. It became an important trade link during China's Han dynasty, around the second century BCE, and remained active for more than a thousand years. The name itself is modern; a German geographer introduced it in the nineteenth century because Chinese silk was one of the most famous goods carried westward.

In fact, very few merchants traveled the entire route. Instead, goods usually moved in stages, passing from one trader to another at oasis towns and market cities. Each merchant covered only a portion of the distance before selling to the next. Along the way, travelers rested at roadside inns called caravanserais, which offered shelter for people and their camels. Silk, paper, and porcelain moved west, while horses, glass, and silver moved east.

The Silk Road carried more than merchandise, however. Religions, technologies, and artistic styles spread along the same routes. Buddhism, for example, traveled from India into China largely through these trading networks. Unfortunately, the exchange was not always beneficial: diseases could also move with caravans, and many historians believe that trade routes helped plague spread across Eurasia in the fourteenth century.

shared.title: How sleep helps us remember
shared.text:
Okay, let's get started. How many of you stayed up late studying for last week's quiz? Yeah, I see a lot of hands. Well, today's topic might change your study habits, because we're going to talk about how sleep helps us form memories.

When you learn something new, say a list of vocabulary words, the memory is fragile at first. Psychologists use the term consolidation for the process that makes a new memory stable and long-lasting. And it turns out that a lot of consolidation happens while you're asleep.

Here's how we think it works. During the day, a brain structure called the hippocampus helps record new experiences. Then, during deep sleep, what's called slow-wave sleep, the brain seems to replay those experiences. In studies with rats, researchers recorded brain cells that fired in a certain pattern while the rats ran through a maze. Later, when the rats were asleep, the same cells fired again in a similar pattern. It's as if the brain was practicing. Over time, this replay seems to help move memories into more permanent storage in the cortex, the outer layer of the brain.

Experiments with people point in the same direction. In a typical study, two groups learn the same material. One group sleeps afterward, and the other stays awake for the same number of hours. When they're tested, the group that slept usually remembers more.

So what does this mean for you? Studying all night and skipping sleep might feel productive, but it can actually undo some of your hard work. Getting a good night's sleep is part of learning.
